ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

The Research Ethics Committee of the [masked for review] provided the ethics approval for Study 4.

Dataset 1 (Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023) used a validated single-item measure of generic conspiracy beliefs (Lantian et al., 2016), in which participants were presented with a preamble describing how official versions of political and social events may hide the truth.
table.formatted: Dataset 1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023)</ref> used a validated single-item measure of generic conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lantian et al., 2016)</ref>, in which participants were presented with a preamble describing how official versions of political and social events may hide the truth.

table.text: In some countries, respondents were compensated with course credit or monetary rewards, with values depending on the local context.
Informed consent was obtained from the participants prior to survey completion.
Participants were US residents aged 18 and older.
Participants (Polish adults) were recruited through an external panel provider (Pollster).

After applying the preregistered exclusion criteria, the final sample comprised 493 participants (51.1% women; M age = 48.52, SD age = 16.97), with 166 of them in the pathogen prevalence condition, 169 in the other-crisis condition, and 158 in the control condition.
Next, participants completed a short, openended task in which they summarized the article, followed by the conspiracy belief measures.
After completing the measures, participants were debriefed.

Participants were presented with three items, e.g., "There are currently many infectious diseases around me," and were asked to rate each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
The analyses of the remaining 490 participants were virtually identical to the previously reported results and all conclusions remained unchanged.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Dataset 1 (Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023) used a validated single-item measure of generic conspiracy beliefs (Lantian et al., 2016), in which participants were presented with a preamble describing how official versions of political and social events may hide the truth.

> In some countries, respondents were compensated with course credit or monetary rewards, with values depending on the local context.

> Informed consent was obtained from the participants prior to survey completion.

> Participants were US residents aged 18 and older.

> Participants (Polish adults) were recruited through an external panel provider (Pollster).

> After applying the preregistered exclusion criteria, the final sample comprised 493 participants (51.1% women; M age = 48.52, SD age = 16.97), with 166 of them in the pathogen prevalence condition, 169 in the other-crisis condition, and 158 in the control condition.

> Next, participants completed a short, openended task in which they summarized the article, followed by the conspiracy belief measures.

> After completing the measures, participants were debriefed.

> Participants were presented with three items, e.g., "There are currently many infectious diseases around me," and were asked to rate each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

> The analyses of the remaining 490 participants were virtually identical to the previously reported results and all conclusions remained unchanged.

Ethics approval statement:

> Research Ethics Committees of [masked for review] provided ethics approvals for Study 2.

> The Research Ethics Committee of the [masked for review] provided the ethics approval for Study 4.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We determined the target sample size with an a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007). According to Biddlestone et al. (2025) in their meta-analysis of motives associated with conspiracy beliefs, correlations between these motives and conspiracy beliefs range from r = .14 to r = .16. We took the lower bound as the expected effect size and converted it to Cohen's f, yielding f = .14. A one-way fixed-effects ANOVA with three groups, α = .05, and power = .80 required 495 participants. We set a recruitment target of 550 participants to retain adequate power after exclusions. Following preregistration, we excluded participants who failed an attention check included in the conspiracy belief items, provided an invalid response to the post-article recall task (answering incorrectly, nonsensically, or offtopic), or left any scale incomplete.

table.title: Historical pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs
table.research_questions:
H1. Higher historical pathogen prevalence (country level) will be associated with higher conspiracy beliefs (individual level).
H2. Higher historical pathogen prevalence (country level) will be associated with colder feelings toward foreigners (individual level).
H3. Colder feelings toward foreigners (individual level) will be associated with higher conspiracy beliefs (individual level).
H4. The association between historical pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs will be mediated by feelings toward foreigners
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: Correlational, cross-sectional design. Data are structured hierarchically with individuals nested within countries.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: The data collection is in progress. As of the date of preregistration, only part of the national teams have collected full samples. The data have not been observed, accessed or analyzed by the author of the preregistration.
table.data_collection_procedures: Data were and will be collected in a large-scale cross-cultural survey. In each country, the local research team determined the sampling method and participant reward. Samples include some student samples and some general-population samples. Participants are at least 18 years old and reside in the country where data are collected.
table.sample_size: We aim to include data from at least 50 countries (as many as possible). Each participating team aims to provide at least 200 good-quality responses (all attention checks passed) per country.
table.sample_size_rationale: At the country level, we aim to include as many countries as possible for power and generalizability. As a heuristic, to achieve .80 power (α = .05) to detect a medium country-level association (r ≈ .40), at least 44 country observations are required; therefore, the minimum target was set at 50 countries, with the goal to exceed this if possible. At the individual level, the minimum target within each country is 200.
table.stopping_rule: Within each country, the participating team will be responsible for stopping data collection but the general rule is that the data collection may be stopped after 200 good quality responses are collected. At the country-level, we will stop the data collection, when all participating teams have finished their data collection.
table.measured_variables:
Measured variables (individual level)

Conspiracy beliefs

Measured with one item from the Bruder et al. (2013) conspiracy mentality scale - "I think that there are secret organizations that greatly influence political decisions."

Attitudes toward foreigners

Measured with a feeling thermometer toward foreigners on a scale ranging from 1 (very cold, negative feelings) to 6 (very warm, positive feelings)

Country-level variable

Historical pathogen prevalence

A country-level historical pathogen prevalence index taken from Fincher et al. (2008)
table.statistical_tests: We will test a 2-1-1 multilevel mediation model with individuals nested within countries (with random intercepts and random slopes).
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will exclude participants who failed the attention check: “Here, please mark number five.” Outliers will be included in the analysis.
table.missing_data_handling:
We will include only respondents who provided complete data on:
the conspiracy beliefs item
the feeling thermometer item

Countries missing the historical pathogen prevalence score will be excluded from the analysis.
table.additional_comments: This preregistration is a part of a large cross-cultural survey including topics such as well-being, societal development, individualism, or foundations of power.

table.title: State-level pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs
table.research_questions: H1: State-level infectious disease prevalence will be positively associated with levels of belief in conspiracy theories (state-level means from Perlis et al., 2025).
table.study_type: Descriptive study: Describing some features of a dataset or sample, but typically not for the purposes of informing a causal effect.
table.study_design_overview: This is a secondary analysis of published, aggregate-level data. No primary data collection will be involved. We will correlate the state-level means of conspiracy beliefs taken from Perlis et al. (2025) with the state-level infectious disease prevalence scores taken from Fincher and Thornhill (2012). The design is cross-sectional with no within-, between-, or repeated-measures components. There is no experimental manipulation, randomization, or counterbalancing.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Conspiracy beliefs data: The data come from the 50-state, nonprobability, web-based survey conducted by the COVID States Project via Pure Spectrum. The survey used state-by-state quotas for age, gender, and race/ethnicity. Participants were US residents aged 18 and older (N = 123,781).

Pathogen prevalence data: State-level infectious disease prevalence scores come from Fincher and Thornhill (2012). This measure aggregates all infectious diseases reported by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for each state from 1993 to 2007, divides by state population, and transforms the result into a z-score.
table.sample_size: The analysis includes data from all 50 US states. The sample size is determined by the design of the original data source.
table.measured_variables:
Conspiracy beliefs were assessed using the American Conspiratorial Thinking Scale (ACTS; Uscinski & Parent, 2014). 

State-level infectious disease prevalence scores were prepared by Fincher and Thornhill (2012).
table.statistical_tests: Bivariate Pearson correlation between state-level infectious disease prevalence (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012) and state-level means of all four ACTS conspiracy items (Perlis et al., 2025).
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We do not plan any exclusions
table.missing_data_handling: The data is already available and does not contain any missing values.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Only people other than the authors have observed the data. At least some of the data that will be used for this analysis plan has been accessed by people other than the authors. However, the authors certify that they have not observed any of that data and will not do so until after this plan is registered.
table.explanation_of_foreknowledge_and_managin: The data on conspiracy beliefs have been published in Perlis et al. (2025). The state-level infectious disease prevalence data were published in Fincher and Thornhill (2012). As of the date of this preregistration, no analysis combining these two datasets has been conducted by the authors of this preregistration.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Indirect inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to examine a potential causal relationship, but is not designed to isolate the specific causal effect. This work may inform causal inference indirectly or advance insight toward future estimation of a causal relationship.
table.indices: To examine conspiracy beliefs, we will use the mean calculated by Perlis et al. (2025) for each state.
table.inference_criteria: We will use α = .05 (two-tailed) as the threshold for statistical significance.

table.title: Pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs – experiment
table.research_questions: We hypothesize that participants exposed to an article describing an infectious-disease outbreak (the pathogen prevalence condition) will report stronger conspiracy beliefs than participants in the neutral control condition (H1). We further test whether this effect is specific to disease-related crises by comparing the pathogen prevalence condition with an other-crisis (regarding the housing crisis) condition; we predict that conspiracy beliefs will be stronger in the pathogen prevalence condition than in the other-crisis condition (H2).
table.study_type: Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
table.blinding: Subjects will not be aware of the assigned treatment during data collection (either because the subjects are not human participants or because of blinding procedures).
table.study_design_overview: Between-subjects experimental design with three levels: pathogen prevalence vs. other-crisis vs. control.
table.data_collection_procedures: The target population is adults living in Poland. Participants will be recruited online through a panel administered by an external company and will complete the study on Qualtrics. To be eligible, participants must be at least 18 years old and must complete the study on a desktop computer or laptop, as the survey is not available on mobile devices. After consent and demographic questions, Qualtrics will randomly assign each participant to one of the three conditions (pathogen prevalence, other-crisis, control) in approximately equal proportions. Recruitment will continue until 550 complete responses meeting the inclusion criteria are obtained.
table.sample_size: Target sample size: 550 participants (183 per condition).
table.sample_size_rationale: We anchored the expected effect size to the meta-analysis by Biddlestone et al. (2025), which examined motivations for conspiracy beliefs and reported correlation coefficients ranging from r = 0.14 to r = 0.16. Converting the lower bound (r = 0.14) to Cohen's f yields an expected effect of approximately f = 0.14 for our main manipulation. A power analysis using G*Power indicated that detecting an effect of f = 0.14 with alpha = 0.05 and power = 0.80 requires 495 participants. We plan to recruit 550 participants to account for potential exclusions due to missing data or failed attention checks.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection will continue until the target sample size is reached.
table.manipulated_variables: Experimental condition (pathogen prevalence vs. other-crisis vs. control), operationalized through the newspaper-style article participants read.
table.measured_variables:
Conspiracy beliefs

Generic Conspiracist Beliefs scale (Kay & Slovic, 2026); and a single item assessing vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs (Toribio-Florez et al., 2025).

Manipulation check

Perceived pathogen prevalence (3 items assessing perceived likelihood of catching an infectious disease and the perceived presence of infectious disease in one's immediate surroundings).
table.statistical_tests:
Manipulation check: A one-way ANOVA on perceived pathogen prevalence with experimental condition as the between-subjects factor, followed by Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons. We expect the pathogen prevalence condition to score higher than the control and other-crisis conditions.

H1 and H2: A one-way ANOVA on each measure of conspiracy beliefs with experimental condition as the between-subjects factor, followed by Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons. H1 is tested by the pathogen prevalence vs. control comparison, and H2 by the pathogen prevalence vs. other-crisis comparison.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participants will be excluded if they:
- fail the embedded attention check (an item instructing them to select a specific scale value)
- provide an invalid response to the post-article memory task (responses that are incorrect, nonsensical, or off-topic will be considered invalid)
- do not complete all items in a scale.
table.missing_data_handling: Analyses will be conducted on complete cases. As stated in the exclusion criteria, participants who do not complete every item of a scale will be removed from analyses, so each index will be computed only for participants with full item-level data.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Direct inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to infer or estimate a causal relationship between two or more variables. It is designed specifically for the purposes of causal inference or identification.
table.indices: The Generic Conspiracist Beliefs scale index will be computed as the mean of the items, with higher scores indicating stronger conspiracy beliefs. The manipulation-check index, perceived pathogen prevalence, will be computed as the mean of its three items, with higher scores indicating greater perceived presence of, and likelihood of contracting, infectious disease in the participant's surroundings. Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) will be reported for each index.
table.transformations: No centering, standardization, or other transformation of the outcome variables is planned.
table.inference_criteria: All tests will use alpha = .05. Each one-way ANOVA begins with the omnibus F test, followed by two-tailed Tukey HSD comparisons, which control the family-wise error rate across the three pairwise contrasts. We will report eta-squared for each omnibus effect and Cohen's d with 95% confidence intervals for each comparison.
table.exploratory_analyses: As robustness checks, we will (1) examine whether results hold after excluding participants who report having previously heard media reports about the hantavirus described in the pathogen prevalence article, and (2) code the open-ended post-conspiracy measures responses for spontaneous mentions of COVID-19 and re-run the main analyses excluding participants who mentioned COVID-19. The latter check verifies that any effect of the pathogen prevalence manipulation is not driven by participants spontaneously thinking about the COVID-19 pandemic rather than the infectious-disease prevalence described in the article.

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 297 columns across 17 data files.
#### Issues Identified

16 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

29 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **29 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 17 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 16 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  12 of 16 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  17 installable dependencies detected.
- 1442 statistics stored from the extracted output; 19 of 37 reported tests matched (51.4%).

ethics_statements: Research Ethics Committees of [masked for review] provided ethics approvals for Study 2.
The Research Ethics Committee of the [masked for review] provided the ethics approval for Study 4.
live_data_statements: Dataset 1 (Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023) used a validated single-item measure of generic conspiracy beliefs (Lantian et al., 2016), in which participants were presented with a preamble describing how official versions of political and social events may hide the truth.
In some countries, respondents were compensated with course credit or monetary rewards, with values depending on the local context.
Informed consent was obtained from the participants prior to survey completion.
Participants were US residents aged 18 and older.
Participants (Polish adults) were recruited through an external panel provider (Pollster).

After applying the preregistered exclusion criteria, the final sample comprised 493 participants (51.1% women; M age = 48.52, SD age = 16.97), with 166 of them in the pathogen prevalence condition, 169 in the other-crisis condition, and 158 in the control condition.
Next, participants completed a short, openended task in which they summarized the article, followed by the conspiracy belief measures.
After completing the measures, participants were debriefed.

Participants were presented with three items, e.g., "There are currently many infectious diseases around me," and were asked to rate each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
The analyses of the remaining 490 participants were virtually identical to the previously reported results and all conclusions remained unchanged.

report:
This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 16 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:16, File = c("Study 1-supplementary analyses.Rmd", 
"Study 1.Rmd", "Study-1-supplementary-analyses.R", "Study-1.R", 
"Study2-supplementary analyses-murray.R", "Study2-supplementary analyses-murray.Rmd", 
"Study2-supplementary analyses.R", "Study2-supplementary analyses.Rmd", 
"Study2.R", "Study2.Rmd", "Study 3.Rmd", "Study-3.R", "Study4-supplementary analyses.Rmd", 
"Study4-supplementary-analyses.R", "Study4.R", "Study4.Rmd"), 
    "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", 
    "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", 
    "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", 
    "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", 
    "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric"
    )), row.names = c(NA, -16L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
**2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `jespfocal.csv` to `../jespfocal.csv` (in Study 1-supplementary analyses.Rmd); `jespfocal.csv` to `../jespfocal.csv` (in Study-1-supplementary-analyses.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 16 scripts: 12 ran without error, 0 errored, 4 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

#### SPSS data without syntax
An SPSS data file (`.sav`/`.por`) is present but **no SPSS syntax file (`.sps`) was found**, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the analysis in **jamovi** (`.omv`) or **JASP** (`.jasp`) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

text.text: Conspiracy beliefs vary substantially across countries and regions, yet the ecological factors underlying this variation remain largely unexplored.
Drawing on behavioral immune system theory, which suggests that pathogen threat can heighten vigilance toward potential dangers, we examined whether pathogen prevalence predicts conspiracy beliefs.
Study 1 analyzed four cross-national datasets (20-32 countries) and found that conspiracy beliefs were higher in countries with greater historical pathogen prevalence.

Study 2 tested this relationship in a preregistered study using a larger sample (N = 15,503 from 55 countries) and found that historical pathogen prevalence predicted higher levels of conspiracy beliefs.
Study 3 extended these findings to the US state level using data from 123,781 participants across 50 states.
Finally, Study 4 (N = 493) experimentally manipulated perceived pathogen prevalence and found causal effects on generic and vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs.
These findings extend behavioral immune system research by relating pathogen-rich ecologies to contemporary conspiracy thinking.

Keywords: Conspiracy beliefs, pathogen prevalence, behavioral immune system Conspiracy theories, defined as explanations attributing significant events to secret plots by powerful, malevolent actors (Douglas et al., 2017), persist across historical eras and cultural contexts (van Prooijen & Douglas, 2017; van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018).

text.text: These beliefs undermine public health efforts

Research on predictors of conspiracy beliefs spans multiple levels of analysis, from individual-level personality traits, cognitive styles, and motivational needs (e.g., Biddlestone et al., 2025; Bowes et al., 2023; Stasielowicz, 2022) to the characteristics of societies themselves.

text.text: For example, large-scale cross-national surveys revealed substantial variation across countries (Hornsey, Bierwiaczonek, et al., 2023; Hornsey & Pearson, 2022) and subsequent studies found conspiracy beliefs are higher in countries with greater corruption (Alper, 2023), lower GDP per capita (Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023), less societal freedom (Siemiątkowski et al., 2026), and greater World War II losses (Bilewicz et al., 2024).

text.text: Ecological factors, however, have received less attention, though Zhao et al. (2024) found that natural disaster risk predicts conspiracy beliefs across 67 countries.

text.text: One ecological factor studied extensively in cross-cultural psychology is pathogen prevalence (Fincher et al., 2008; Murray & Schaller, 2010).
text.formatted: One ecological factor studied extensively in cross-cultural psychology is pathogen prevalence <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fincher et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Murray & Schaller, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Pathogens have posed persistent, high-stakes survival threats throughout human history, and their prevalence appears to have shaped cross-cultural differences in social organization and values, including collectivism (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012; Schaller & Murray, 2011), conformity (Murray & Schaller, 2016), traditionalism (Tybur et al., 2016), and negative attitudes toward outgroups (O'Shea et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Pathogens have posed persistent, high-stakes survival threats throughout human history, and their prevalence appears to have shaped cross-cultural differences in social organization and values, including collectivism <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fincher & Thornhill, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schaller & Murray, 2011)</ref>, conformity <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Murray & Schaller, 2016)</ref>, traditionalism <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Tybur et al., 2016)</ref>, and negative attitudes toward outgroups <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(O'Shea et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Pathogen prevalence has accordingly been linked to political attitudes more broadly, predicting both authoritarian personalities and governance (Murray et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Pathogen prevalence has accordingly been linked to political attitudes more broadly, predicting both authoritarian personalities and governance <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Murray et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this work, we propose that environments with higher pathogen prevalence foster susceptibility to conspiratorial thinking because they create prolonged threat and vigilance toward potential sources of harm.
The behavioral immune system framework explains how pathogen threat shapes individual-level cognition.

Alongside physiological immunity, humans evolved mechanisms that detect cues of potential infection and motivate behavioral avoidance (Murray & Schaller, 2016; Neuberg et al., 2011; Schaller & Park, 2011).
text.formatted: Alongside physiological immunity, humans evolved mechanisms that detect cues of potential infection and motivate behavioral avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Murray & Schaller, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Neuberg et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Schaller & Park, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These responses involve heightened disgust toward potential contamination cues, more pronounced when the source is unfamiliar (Oaten et al., 2009), and increased vigilance and caution in social interaction (Murray & Schaller, 2016; Schaller & Park, 2011).
text.formatted: These responses involve heightened disgust toward potential contamination cues, more pronounced when the source is unfamiliar <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Oaten et al., 2009)</ref>, and increased vigilance and caution in social interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Murray & Schaller, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Schaller & Park, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The system operates through an oversensitive "smoke detector" logic, responding to ambiguous cues of possible pathogen risk even at the cost of frequent false alarms, because infection can have severe consequences (Nesse, 2005; Schaller & Park, 2011).
text.formatted: The system operates through an oversensitive "smoke detector" logic, responding to ambiguous cues of possible pathogen risk even at the cost of frequent false alarms, because infection can have severe consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Nesse, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Schaller & Park, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This mindset fosters hypervigilance and suspicion under elevated disease threat, as chronic and primed disease concerns bias individuals to overdetect disease cues in others (Miller & Maner, 2012).
text.formatted: This mindset fosters hypervigilance and suspicion under elevated disease threat, as chronic and primed disease concerns bias individuals to overdetect disease cues in others <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Miller & Maner, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These states may extend beyond avoiding infection to detecting coordinated threats from others.

Because hostile coalitions act in secret, a miss can cost more than a false alarm, so suspecting coordinated intent behind ambiguous cues lets a threat be anticipated rather than endured, an error-management logic directly linked to conspiracy belief formation (van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018).
text.formatted: Because hostile coalitions act in secret, a miss can cost more than a false alarm, so suspecting coordinated intent behind ambiguous cues lets a threat be anticipated rather than endured, an error-management logic directly linked to conspiracy belief formation <ref type="bibr">(van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: At the cultural level, parasite-stress theory proposes that historically high pathogen prevalence contributed to enduring cross-cultural differences in social structures and values, particularly norms governing group boundaries and social conformity (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012; Thornhill & Fincher, 2014a , 2014b).
text.formatted: At the cultural level, parasite-stress theory proposes that historically high pathogen prevalence contributed to enduring cross-cultural differences in social structures and values, particularly norms governing group boundaries and social conformity <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fincher & Thornhill, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Thornhill & Fincher, 2014a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">, 2014b)</ref>.

text.text: We propose that the consequences discussed below create environments fostering conspiracy belief endorsement.

Societies under generations of infectious disease pressure developed norms emphasizing in-group cohesion (Fincher et al., 2008; Fincher & Thornhill, 2012), conformity (Murray et al., 2011), limited openness to experience (Schaller & Murray, 2008), avoidance of contact with outgroup members (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012; Thornhill & Fincher, 2014b), and traditionalism, the aspect of political ideology concerning adherence to group norms (Tybur et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Societies under generations of infectious disease pressure developed norms emphasizing in-group cohesion <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fincher et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Fincher & Thornhill, 2012)</ref>, conformity <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Murray et al., 2011)</ref>, limited openness to experience <ref type="bibr">(Schaller & Murray, 2008)</ref>, avoidance of contact with outgroup members <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fincher & Thornhill, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Thornhill & Fincher, 2014b)</ref>, and traditionalism, the aspect of political ideology concerning adherence to group norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Tybur et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Most of these factors correlate with conspiracy beliefs (Adam-Troian et al., 2021; Bowes et al., 2023; Cookson et al., 2021; Jolley et al., 2020; van Prooijen & Song, 2021).
text.formatted: Most of these factors correlate with conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adam-Troian et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bowes et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Cookson et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Jolley et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">van Prooijen & Song, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, regions with higher historical prevalence exhibit stronger in-group assortative sociality, indexed by family ties and religiosity (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012), a narrower "radius of trust" confined to close in-group members (Kammas & Sarantides, 2024), and moral vitalism, the belief in contagious and agentic spiritual forces of evil (Bastian et al., 2019).

text.text: Within the United States, state-level disease prevalence predicts racial prejudice (O'Shea et al., 2020), and experimentally salient disease threat increases negative attitudes toward foreign immigrant groups (Faulkner et al., 2004).

text.text: Perceived vulnerability to disease likewise relates to stronger ethnocentric attitudes (Navarrete & Fessler, 2006).

text.text: These adaptations may have reduced infection risk by limiting exposure.

Pathogen prevalence shapes not only values but also social network structure, as high-pathogen environments favor low-diffusion networks with strong in-group ties and limited contact with outsiders (Fogli & Veldkamp, 2021).
text.formatted: Pathogen prevalence shapes not only values but also social network structure, as high-pathogen environments favor low-diffusion networks with strong in-group ties and limited contact with outsiders <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fogli & Veldkamp, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: According to the existential threat model of conspiracy theories (van Prooijen, 2020), distressing circumstances activate epistemic sense-making processes, giving rise to conspiracy beliefs only when antagonistic outgroups are salient.
Pathogen-rich environments may activate this pathway in several ways.
First, chronic disease threat sustains feelings of vulnerability that motivate sense-making.

Because pathogens are invisible and their carriers often unidentifiable, this vulnerability is a diffuse anxiety without a clear object, which motivates attempts to explain the danger and identify who is behind it (van Prooijen, 2020).
Second, outgroup wariness fostered by pathogen avoidance increases the salience of potential antagonists, toward whom conspiratorial suspicions can be directed.

Conspiracy detection may itself be adaptive, predisposing individuals to suspect hostile alliances among outgroup members acting secretly against their in-group, especially under perceived intergroup threat (van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018).
text.formatted: Conspiracy detection may itself be adaptive, predisposing individuals to suspect hostile alliances among outgroup members acting secretly against their in-group, especially under perceived intergroup threat <ref type="bibr">(van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Because high pathogen prevalence promotes threat sensitivity (Schaller & Park, 2011) and sharper intergroup boundaries (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012), it may amplify both the motivation to seek explanations and the tendency to attribute coordinated malevolent intent to outgroups.
text.formatted: Because high pathogen prevalence promotes threat sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Schaller & Park, 2011)</ref> and sharper intergroup boundaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fincher & Thornhill, 2012)</ref>, it may amplify both the motivation to seek explanations and the tendency to attribute coordinated malevolent intent to outgroups.

text.text: Moreover, perceived threat, anxiety, and the belief that the world is dangerous are among the most consistent meta-analytic correlates of conspiracy beliefs (Biddlestone et al., 2025; Bowes et al., 2023), and more anxious individuals experiencing greater existential threat endorse conspiracy theories more strongly (Liekefett et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Moreover, perceived threat, anxiety, and the belief that the world is dangerous are among the most consistent meta-analytic correlates of conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Biddlestone et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bowes et al., 2023)</ref>, and more anxious individuals experiencing greater existential threat endorse conspiracy theories more strongly <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Liekefett et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Building on the behavioral immune system framework and parasite-stress theory, we propose that conspiracy beliefs are stronger where infectious diseases have been more prevalent, and that heightening perceived pathogen prevalence increases their endorsement.
We tested this proposition in four studies that differ in level of analysis, operationalization, and design.

Study 1 examined whether historical pathogen prevalence (Fincher et al., 2008) is associated with country-level conspiracy beliefs in four existing cross-national datasets that measured conspiracy beliefs in different ways, from the endorsement of specific conspiracy theories to a generalized conspiracy mentality.
text.formatted: Study 1 examined whether historical pathogen prevalence <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fincher et al., 2008)</ref> is associated with country-level conspiracy beliefs in four existing cross-national datasets that measured conspiracy beliefs in different ways, from the endorsement of specific conspiracy theories to a generalized conspiracy mentality.

text.text: Study 2 tested the same association in a larger, preregistered study with individual-level data from 55 countries.

Because cross-national comparisons are open to many alternative explanations, Study 3 examined whether the association also holds within a single country, relating state-level infectious disease prevalence to state-level conspiracy beliefs across the 50 US states.
Because Studies 1 to 3 are correlational, Study 4 tested the direction of the relationship experimentally.

Participants read a newspaper-style article that heightened perceived pathogen prevalence, a neutral article, or an article about a societal crisis unrelated to infectious disease, which allowed us to examine whether conspiracy beliefs respond to pathogen threat specifically rather than to crisis information in general.
Across the four studies, we expected higher pathogen prevalence to be associated with stronger conspiracy beliefs.
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the studies, and we follow the JARS (Appelbaum et al., 2018).

The primary aim of Study 1 was to examine the relationship between historical pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs.

We conducted secondary analyses of four existing cross-national datasets, which were previously used by Hornsey and Pearson (2022), matching the country-level means of conspiracy beliefs reported in that work with historical pathogen prevalence scores.

text.text: Each dataset employed different measures of conspiracy beliefs.

This multi-dataset approach enabled us to evaluate the consistency of the hypothesized association across various operationalizations of conspiracy beliefs, ranging from the endorsement of specific conspiracy theories to the conspiracy mentality.

Countries served as the unit of analysis, consistent with the treatment of nations as meaningful cultural units whose aggregated scores capture central tendencies while averaging out individual-level noise (Akaliyski et al., 2021).

text.text: We hypothesized that historical pathogen prevalence would be positively associated with conspiracy beliefs.

We tested this hypothesis across four datasets, each employing a different measure: generic conspiracy beliefs, belief in specific globally recognized conspiracy theories, conspiracy mentality, and belief in a second set of globally recognized conspiracy theories.
We analyzed four cross-national datasets, each of which provided a different operationalization of conspiracy beliefs (see Hornsey & Pearson, 2022, for an overview).

text.text: Conspiracy beliefs.

Dataset 1 (Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023) used a validated single-item measure of generic conspiracy beliefs (Lantian et al., 2016), in which participants were presented with a preamble describing how official versions of political and social events may hide the truth.
text.formatted: Dataset 1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023)</ref> used a validated single-item measure of generic conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lantian et al., 2016)</ref>, in which participants were presented with a preamble describing how official versions of political and social events may hide the truth.

text.text: Then, they were asked to rate their agreement with the statement, "I think that the official version of the events given by the authorities very often hides the truth" on a scale ranging from 1 (completely false) to 9 (completely true).

Dataset 2 (Hornsey et al., 2018) assessed endorsement of four globally recognized conspiracy theories (for more details see Table S1 in the Supplementary Materials) using a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
text.formatted: Dataset 2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hornsey et al., 2018)</ref> assessed endorsement of four globally recognized conspiracy theories (for more details see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> in the Supplementary Materials) using a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

text.text: Dataset 3 (Imhoff et al., 2022) used the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (Bruder et al., 2013) to measure a generalized tendency to suspect hidden conspiracies behind significant societal events on an 11-point scale ranging from 0 (certainly not) to 10 (certain).
text.formatted: Dataset 3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Imhoff et al., 2022)</ref> used the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bruder et al., 2013)</ref> to measure a generalized tendency to suspect hidden conspiracies behind significant societal events on an 11-point scale ranging from 0 (certainly not) to 10 (certain).

text.text: Finally, dataset 4 (YouGov, 2020) measured belief in five globally recognized conspiracy theories (see the Supplementary Materials).
Respondents indicated their level of agreement on a scale ranging from 1 (definitely false) to 4 (definitely true).
These instruments capture related but distinct constructs.

Generic conspiracy beliefs (dataset 1) reflect a general distrust of official accounts (Lantian et al., 2016), conspiracy mentality (dataset 3) reflects a generalized readiness to interpret events as the product of secret plots (Imhoff & Bruder, 2014), and belief in specific conspiracy theories (datasets 2 and 4) reflects the endorsement of particular claims.

text.text: Observing the same association across these constructs would therefore indicate that it does not depend on any single operationalization.
We used Fincher et al.'s (2008) index to operationalize country-level historical pathogen prevalence.
text.formatted: We used <ref type="bibr">Fincher et al.'s (2008)</ref> index to operationalize country-level historical pathogen prevalence.

text.text: This index compiles historical prevalence estimates for nine infectious diseases (leishmaniasis, trypanosomiasis, malaria, schistosomiasis, filariasis, leprosy, dengue, typhus, and tuberculosis) across geopolitical regions, estimated primarily from mid-twentieth-century epidemiological atlases that record disease burden before the widespread availability of modern medicine (see Fincher et al., 2008, for details of the coding).

text.text: Scores in the full index range from -1.29 to 1.28, with higher values indicating greater historical pathogen prevalence.
The countries included in the samples used covered most of this range in all four datasets.

To ensure the robustness of our findings, we replicated all analyses using another nine-item historical disease prevalence index developed by Murray and Schaller (2010), which applies the same coding procedure to the same nine diseases and atlases but rates all regions anew and extends coverage to 230 geopolitical regions.

Study 1 provided initial evidence for a positive association between historical pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs across multiple cross-national datasets.
Study 2 built on that evidence using a larger cross-national dataset with individual-level data, which allowed us to estimate a multilevel model.
We predicted that higher historical pathogen prevalence measured at the country level would be associated with higher levels of conspiracy beliefs.

text.text: Although the preregistration specified a 2-1-1 multilevel mediation model in which country-level historical pathogen prevalence predicted individual-level conspiracy beliefs indirectly through attitudes toward foreigners, measured with a feeling thermometer, this article reports only the preregistered country-level association (H1).
The preregistered mediation analyses (H2, H3, and H4) are reported in full in the Supplementary Materials and are not discussed in the main text.
We made this decision because there is evidence that the association between attitudes toward foreigners and conspiracy beliefs might operate in both directions.

Apart from our rationale for the effect from negative attitudes toward foreigners to conspiracy beliefs, experimental work indicated that exposure to intergroup conspiracy theories increases prejudice toward the group implicated and, indirectly, toward uninvolved outgroups (Jolley et al., 2020), so colder attitudes toward foreigners may follow from conspiracy beliefs as readily as precede them.

text.text: Data for Study 2 were collected in 2024-2026 as part of a larger cross-cultural study examining various topics, including well-being, societal development, and authoritarianism.
All materials were first prepared in English by the last author with input from co-authors.
Next, all collaborators adapted and translated the survey using a back-translation method to then collect data in their respective countries.
The required sample size for each country was set as N = 200.
Eventually, some samples were smaller and some were larger.
The final database included a mix of community, student, quota-based, and mixed samples.
In some countries, respondents were compensated with course credit or monetary rewards, with values depending on the local context.
Informed consent was obtained from the participants prior to survey completion.
The full list of countries with the descriptives of samples in each of them is presented in the Supplementary Materials (Table S5).

text.text: We collected data from 37,291 participants residing in 70 countries.

After excluding participants who had missing data on the studied variables or failed at least one of the eight attention checks embedded in the survey as well as countries for which historical pathogen prevalence data was not available, the final sample consisted of 15,503 participants from 55 countries (60.6% women, 35.5% men, 0.8% who declared other gender, and 3.2% who decided not to indicate their gender; M age = 30.37, SD age = 13.44).
Historical pathogen prevalence was measured using the same index as in Study 1 (Fincher et al., 2008; range in this sample -1.29 to 1.28).

text.text: Studies 1 and 2 established a positive association between historical pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs across countries using multiple cross-national datasets and various measures of conspiracy beliefs.
However, this cross-national design does not address whether the same pattern holds within a single country, where cultural, linguistic, and institutional factors are more consistent.
If the relationship between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs reflects a general ecological dynamic, it should also emerge when examining regional variation within a single country.
Study 3 tested this prediction using data from the United States and examining the association between state-level infectious disease prevalence and state-level conspiracy beliefs.

Studies 1-3 provided evidence for a positive relationship between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs across countries and US states.
However, because these designs were correlational, they cannot establish the direction of the relationship.
Study 4 employed an experimental design to test whether heightened perceived pathogen prevalence increases conspiracy beliefs.
Participants read one of three newspaper-style articles.

The pathogen prevalence article described a novel hantavirus outbreak; the other-crisis article described a societal crisis unrelated to infectious disease (housing crisis); and the control condition article described a neutral topic (urban transportation).
Hantavirus received media attention in spring 2026, when an outbreak on a cruise ship was attributed to human-tohuman transmission (see e.g., Roberts, 2026).
text.formatted: Hantavirus received media attention in spring 2026, when an outbreak on a cruise ship was attributed to human-tohuman transmission (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Roberts, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We expected participants in the heightened pathogen prevalence condition to report stronger conspiracy beliefs than those in the control condition (H1).
The other-crisis condition allowed us to examine whether the effect of the manipulation is specific to disease salience or if it is a response to information about any kind of crisis.
Therefore, we also expected conspiracy beliefs to be stronger in the heightened pathogen prevalence condition than in the other-crisis condition (H2).
The hypotheses, design, and analytic approach were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/v9qyx/overview?view_only=ec3b61033c1a4e8b923fadab71ddbcb3).

text.text: Participants (Polish adults) were recruited through an external panel provider (Pollster).
To avoid issues with visibility of the articles they had to complete the study on a computer.
We collected data from 533 participants.

After applying the preregistered exclusion criteria, the final sample comprised 493 participants (51.1% women; M age = 48.52, SD age = 16.97), with 166 of them in the pathogen prevalence condition, 169 in the other-crisis condition, and 158 in the control condition.
We determined the target sample size with an a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007).

A one-way fixed-effects ANOVA with three groups, α = .05, and power = .80 required 495 participants.
We set a recruitment target of 550 participants to retain adequate power after exclusions.

Following preregistration, we excluded participants who failed an attention check included in the conspiracy belief items, provided an invalid response to the post-article recall task (answering incorrectly, nonsensically, or offtopic), or left any scale incomplete.
The study was administered online through Qualtrics.
After providing informed consent, participants reported their demographics.
Then, they were randomly assigned to one of three conditions and read the corresponding article.
To encourage careful reading, the option to continue was disabled for three minutes.
Next, participants completed a short, openended task in which they summarized the article, followed by the conspiracy belief measures.
Next, they described what they had been thinking about while reading and completed the perceived pathogen prevalence items.
Finally, they were asked whether they had heard of Hantavirus before taking part in the study.
All three articles that served as the manipulation stimuli were written for this study and formatted to resemble reports from an online news service.
The articles were matched in terms of length and structure, and each included quotations attributed to experts.
The article in the pathogen prevalence condition described an outbreak of a novel, human-transmissible hantavirus, as well as rising antibiotic resistance.
The article in the other-crisis condition described a housing market crisis and related infrastructure failures.
The control condition article described urban transportation and cycling.
The full texts of the three articles with translations are provided in the Supplementary Materials (Figures S6-S8).
text.formatted: The full texts of the three articles with translations are provided in the Supplementary Materials (Figures <ref type="figure">S6-S8</ref>).

text.text: After completing the measures, participants were debriefed.

The debriefing explained that the articles had been prepared for research purposes only and did not describe a current public health threat, and directed participants to official public health sources.

Generic conspiracist beliefs (ɑ = .84) were measured using the five-item Generic Conspiracist Beliefs Scale (Kay & Slovic, 2023), which is a shortened version of Brotherton et al.'s (2013) 15-item scale.

Vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs were measured with a single item (Toribio-Florez et al., 2025): "Scientists work together to cover up the dangers of vaccines" which was rated on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

text.text: Perceived pathogen prevalence (ɑ = .83) was measured as a manipulation check.

Participants were presented with three items, e.g., "There are currently many infectious diseases around me," and were asked to rate each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
The full list of items is presented in the Supplementary Materials.
We analyzed the data using one-way ANOVAs with Tukey HSD comparisons.
First, we tested the effectiveness of the manipulation by comparing perceived pathogen prevalence across the three conditions.
Then, we tested our hypotheses about generic conspiracist beliefs by comparing the pathogen prevalence condition with the control condition (H1) and the other-crisis condition (H2).
The vaccine conspiracy belief item was analyzed in the same way.
We preregistered two robustness checks.
Since prior familiarity with the disease could weaken the manipulation, we planned to repeat the analyses after excluding participants who reported having heard of the Hantavirus before the study.

Additionally, because thinking of experience during the COVID-19 pandemic could influence responses to an article about infectious diseases, we planned to code open-ended responses for spontaneous mentions of the COVID-19 pandemic and to repeat the analyses after excluding participants who mentioned it.
The results of these analyses are presented in the Supplementary Materials.
A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of condition on perceived pathogen prevalence, F(2, 490) = 5.39, p = .005, η² = .02.

Tukey HSD comparisons showed that participants in the pathogen prevalence condition perceived a higher prevalence of pathogens (M = 3.34, SE = 0.10) than those in the control condition (M = 2.95, SE = 0.11; p = .021, d = 0.30, 95% CI [0.08, 0.52]) and the other-crisis condition (M = 2.91, SE = 0.10; p = .008, d = 0.33, 95% CI [0.11, 0.54]).
The control and other-crisis conditions did not differ from each other (p = .961, d = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.25]).
A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of condition, F(2, 490) = 8.28, p < .001, η² = .03.

text.text: Also, in line with H2, they reported higher levels of generic conspiracist beliefs than participants in the othercrisis condition (M = 2.69, SE = 0.09; p = .006, d = 0.34, 95% CI [0.12, 0.55]).
The difference between the control and other-crisis conditions was not significant (p = .691, d = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.31, 0.13]).
The same pattern emerged in the case of the vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs, for which we also found a significant main effect of condition, F(2, 490) = 9.82, p < .001, η² = .04.

text.text: In the first analysis, participants who spontaneously mentioned the COVID-19 pandemic in the open-ended item were excluded.
Only three of the 493 responses contained such mentions.
The analyses of the remaining 490 participants were virtually identical to the previously reported results and all conclusions remained unchanged.
The second analysis excluded participants who reported having heard of Hantavirus before the study.
Of the 493 participants, 305 (61.9%) reported prior familiarity, leaving 188 for this analysis.
Retention did not differ significantly across conditions.
Within this subsample, the manipulation remained effective.
Participants in the pathogen prevalence condition perceived a higher prevalence of pathogens than those in the control and other-crisis conditions.
However, the effects of the condition on generic conspiracist beliefs and vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs were not significant.
Because only 38.1% of the sample was retained, these analyses had limited power to detect effects of the size observed in the full sample.
This research examined the relationship between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs.
Study 1 found higher endorsement of various conspiracy beliefs in countries with higher historical pathogen prevalence.
Both Study 2, which included a larger cross-national sample, and Study 3, which examined US states, replicated the findings of Study 1.

Finally, Study 4 found that manipulating perceived pathogen prevalence increased generic and vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs compared to a neutral article and one about an unrelated societal crisis.

These findings add disease ecology to the societal characteristics associated with conspiracy beliefs, alongside greater corruption (Alper, 2023), weaker economic performance (Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023), lower societal freedom (Siemiątkowski et al., 2026), and wartime losses (Bilewicz et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These findings add disease ecology to the societal characteristics associated with conspiracy beliefs, alongside greater corruption <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alper, 2023)</ref>, weaker economic performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023)</ref>, lower societal freedom <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Siemiątkowski et al., 2026)</ref>, and wartime losses <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bilewicz et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, pathogen prevalence was examined in three forms, differing in timescale and aggregation level.
The country-level indices summarize disease burden accumulated across generations, describing the ecological context in which a population developed (Fincher et al., 2008; Murray & Schaller, 2010).
text.formatted: The country-level indices summarize disease burden accumulated across generations, describing the ecological context in which a population developed <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fincher et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Murray & Schaller, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The US state-level index reflects incidence recorded by public health surveillance in recent decades (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012).
text.formatted: The US state-level index reflects incidence recorded by public health surveillance in recent decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fincher & Thornhill, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The experimental manipulation concerned how prevalent the disease appeared when measured.

These operationalizations are not identical, and their convergence does not prove a single underlying process, but it does suggest that the association is not confined to one index, timescale, or level of measurement.
The behavioral immune system framework explains why pathogen prevalence consistently matters across these levels.
Evolved pathogen-avoidance mechanisms shape intergroup attitudes by promoting wariness toward unfamiliar others where disease risk is high (Murray & Schaller, 2016; Schaller & Park, 2011).
text.formatted: Evolved pathogen-avoidance mechanisms shape intergroup attitudes by promoting wariness toward unfamiliar others where disease risk is high <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Murray & Schaller, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Schaller & Park, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that this legacy may extend to conspiratorial thinking, possibly because environments of persistent infectious disease foster stronger in-group boundaries and suspicion of outsiders and, given that disease carriers cannot be identified by sight, of hidden agents within one's own society.

This aligns with van Prooijen's (2020) existential threat model, in which conspiracy beliefs emerge when existential threats trigger sense-making in the presence of antagonistic outgroups, because pathogen prevalence is a historically persistent ecological stressor that simultaneously heightens existential uncertainty and outgroup vigilance.
The experimental results also suggest the effect is specific to disease threat.
Were the effect a general reaction to unsettling news, the housing-crisis article should also have raised conspiracy beliefs.

Yet that condition was indistinguishable from the neutral-article control on both outcome measures, consistent with accounts in which pathogen cues engage a distinct threat-management system (Neuberg et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Yet that condition was indistinguishable from the neutral-article control on both outcome measures, consistent with accounts in which pathogen cues engage a distinct threat-management system <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Neuberg et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Similar specificity emerged experimentally for intergroup outcomes, with disease salience reducing positive attitudes toward foreign immigrant groups relative to a salient non-disease threat (Faulkner et al., 2004).

text.text: Taken together, the four studies converge on the same association across levels of analysis, measures, and designs.

Because the responsible processes remain unidentified and only the experimental design allows a causal interpretation, this research remains an initial examination, constrained by the limitations outlined below.

Nevertheless, it points toward a line of inquiry treating conspiracy beliefs as shaped not only by immediate political and informational circumstances but also by ecological conditions persisting over time.

If salient disease cues increase conspiratorial thinking, outbreaks could generate not only a public health crisis but also conditions favoring conspiracy theories, undermining the response to the outbreak itself (Bierwiaczonek et al., 2022).
text.formatted: If salient disease cues increase conspiratorial thinking, outbreaks could generate not only a public health crisis but also conditions favoring conspiracy theories, undermining the response to the outbreak itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bierwiaczonek et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its strengths, our research has several limitations.
The macro-level studies were correlational, which limits causal claims.

The experiment addressed the direction of the effect, but did so for perceived rather than historical prevalence, and therefore cannot establish that the process it demonstrates generates the cross-national pattern.
A related caution concerns the non-pathogen crisis comparison.

A single null result indicates that this particular stimulus did not raise conspiracy beliefs, not that non-disease crises are generally ineffective, and testing further crisis types would strengthen the case for specificity.
Additionally, the experimental effects were small to moderate, as expected given that a brief news article is a minimal intervention compared to a lifetime in a disease ecology.
Stronger or repeated manipulations and longitudinal designs tracking conspiracy beliefs as disease salience shifts would determine whether these effects grow and persist under sustained exposure.

Our designs also do not identify the processes through which disease ecology becomes associated with conspiracy beliefs, whether through culturally transmitted norms of in-group cohesion and wariness toward outsiders, through vigilance activated by contemporary disease cues, or through feelings of anxiety.
Furthermore, analyses in Studies 1 and 3 used aggregated scores unadjusted for subsample size in each macro-level unit, a limitation Study 2 addresses with a multilevel model.
Moreover, younger respondents and women were overrepresented in the samples of Studies 1 and 2.
Finally, the available datasets left certain regions underrepresented, most notably Sub-Saharan Africa, where pathogen prevalence has been historically high.
Expanding cross-national research to more countries would allow a more comprehensive evaluation of this framework.
Nonetheless, this research is among the largest cross-national examinations of conspiracy beliefs to date.

The present research demonstrated a positive association between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs across multiple datasets and showed that heightened perceived prevalence increases their endorsement.
These findings provide initial evidence that pathogen-rich ecologies may contribute to contemporary conspiracy thinking.
Two constraints qualify this conclusion.

The macro-level evidence is correlational, so the causal claim rests on a single experiment manipulating perceived rather than historical prevalence, and the included countries and regions underrepresent those with the heaviest historical disease burden.

Nevertheless, the convergence of centuries-long ecological indices and a momentary experimental cue suggest that infectious disease prevalence shaped not only how societies organize but what their members are prepared to believe.
